items.title: Show HN: Klad, a paint app your coding agent can drive (source-available)
items.summary: I've been developing applications for a long time and have turned to game development as well lately. One of the things that frustrated me the most was that using AI agents for game development is very annoying in the art department. Your only options right now are to either use an image genAI model and roll the dice every time you want to make an edit, or have your agent draw with something like vectors. I was looking for an application that would allow me to ask an agent to make a first draft of whatever art I needed with actual brushes, and then be able to go in myself and edit every last stroke or layer that it created. Klad is that application. Written in Rust, it can be fully controlled by an agent through the CLI, and every function is available in a nice UI as well: a brush engine, frame-by-frame animation (and bones/IK), vectors, text layers, colours, layer effects, infinite undo (even after re-opening the file!),… Why I think it's useful for a wider audience: Adobe showed agents editing Photoshop files at MAX this week, with a private beta planned for early 2027. Klad is built on the same core idea, with editable paint strokes as core architecture, and it works today. Clone the repo to try it out: https://github.com/klad-app/klad You can basically point Claude to the repo, ask it to build it, and pick up the drawing skills. Then ask it to make any drawing you want! (After that, you or the agent can change absolutely every brush stroke in the app again, which makes edits a breeze.) The quality of the drawings really depends on the agent you use. I have tried it with Claude Fable 5.2 since it came out on Monday, and the drawings are already quite impressive. I'm confident that this will only improve. I use it every day on Mac, so that definitely works well. It builds on Linux too (tablet pen pressure still needs some work there). Windows builds in CI, I haven't used it there myself yet but I have some reports that it works perfectly fine. Coming up next is support for pixel art. I'm in the testing phase with this right now, and I expect it to go live in the repo sometime this weekend. Klad is source-available rather than open source: free to build and use for individuals and small companies, and I plan to sell pre-built binaries later, the way Aseprite does. The file format, CLI reference and agent skill are MIT. What I want to hear from people who try it: Can your agent work out the CLI without help, and where does it get confused? Can you go in and change one of its strokes easily? The command reference and guides are available at https://klad.studio I'll be here answering any questions about the technical side as well, as it's a pretty interesting challenge to build a performant engine with editable brush strokes that render as paint.

items.title: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
items.summary: Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings. Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer. As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman. I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy. To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp). I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use. Would love to hear what you think about the onboarding and note taking experience :)

items.title: Show HN: Whisperstream – Free, open-source local dictation for Windows
items.summary: Hi HN, I built Whisperstream, a free and open-source dictation app for Windows. You've seen a dozen of these, so what makes it different from all the other dictation apps? - Local cleanup: We're the only free and open source solution on Windows with a finetuned cleanup model. Stream-1 Mini is a Qwen 0.6B finetune for removing filler and applying spoken corrections. Superwhisper is the only Windows app that offers this, is paid, and in our benchmark we outperform their S1 mini with 36% less failures. Benchmark: https://whisperstream.io/stream-1-mini-vs-s1-mini - Agent Speak: Hear or read response summaries from Claude Code or Codex, and speak back directly. Expand to see the full response without switching contexts. The TTS uses Kokoro for highly realistic voices. - Smart Dictionary: Most local dictation apps don't offer dictionary support when using their fine-tuned cleanup model. We trained it into our finetune and use phonetic matching so we only include similar words for boosting. It's GPL-3.0, completely free and now has a Mac version too. Github: https://github.com/lanreal-io/whisperstream/ Demo: https://whisperstream.io/press/demos/launch-2.0-light.gif

items.title: Show HN: Pots – Open-source Grok Bot alternative, used by 6 startups for a month
items.summary: Hi HN, I'm Crokily. Pots is an AI coworker that lives in the chat your team already uses: Slack, Discord, Telegram, or any channel with a Chat SDK adapter. It is MIT-licensed and runs on a machine you give it, with the model you choose. To be honest, the first time I used Grok Bot, its design really impressed me. Unlike OpenClaw before it, it was not just Claude Code connected to a chat app. It truly cared about how it works with people. It felt like a living AI assistant, and working with it was painless. That is the idea I kept learning from the whole time I built Pots: it is not an agent hooked up to a chat channel. It should be a coworker that feels alive and is comfortable to work with. But Grok Bot is only Grok's bot. Which model you get depends on your X subscription, your data and your machine are all in the cloud, and most of all, it is a standalone app, and most of its features serve that app. Pots is a bit different. In Sydney I have talked with quite a few founders. Grok Bot is good, and it helps them a lot with their personal tasks. But when I asked who had actually put Grok Bot into their company's work to make their startup team faster, nobody had. So I think Pots is in a different place from Grok Bot, and from most open-source Grok Bot alternatives: it grew out of what real startup teams need. Before I open-sourced it, 6 small startups I met at startup events had been using it with me for over a month. Pots is built first for the channels startup teams already work in, not for an app of its own, so most of what it does serves the places where you actually work. The teams use Pots as a middle layer: a CEO talks ideas through with the team in chat, Pots listens, and then it builds a prototype that both sides can check. They use Pots for competitor research: because Pots runs inside their channels, it knows their product well. Not only the GitHub repo, but the team's daily discussions and what the team cares about. Pots has been listening quietly the whole time, so it knows the product with no setup at all. It also works well with each channel: it talks to people with the channel's own controls, like Slack and Discord buttons and cards, and when it hands over something complex, it deploys a page with its built-in server so everyone sees it in a better form. So Pots is different from Grok Bot and from most open-source alternatives. It came out of what real startup teams need. Its channel features start from what each company's work needs, and it can join your real work setup with no setup and still do well, instead of being one more app that nobody uses and that is hard to start with. And it ran in real business for a while before I cleaned it up and open-sourced it. The difference from Grok Bot is also exactly why I made Pots an open-source Grok Bot alternative. I have OpenAI and Claude subscriptions with plenty of quota, and my own servers, so I don't want an X subscription to limit me. I want to use whatever model I want and do whatever I want. I can even switch to an open model, and none of my data goes into anyone's pocket. Try it (Node 24+, macOS, Linux or Windows): the easiest way is to ask your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) to read docs/for-agents.md in the repo and set up Pots for you. Or by hand: npm install -g pi-durable-bot, then pots init. I'd love feedback, especially on how it decides when to act.
